newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Leader falls victim to ceaseless Tajik violence.
newsitem.headline: Leader falls victim to ceaseless Tajik violence.

text.p: A storm of shootings and bombings in Tajikistan caught up with its embattled president in a grenade attack on Wednesday, dampening hopes of an end to the violence that has marked the ex-Soviet state since independence.

President Imomali Rakhmonov, the director of a cotton collective in Soviet times, has staggered from crisis to crisis during his four-year rule, most of which has been spent fighting a bitter civil war.

The attack in the northern town of Khudjand, which left him limping after being wounded in the legs, must have brought home only too painfully his slippery grip on the chronically unstable republic of 5.7 million.
"This is a bad event," said a western diplomat based in the Tajik capital, Dushanbe. "This is a country with far too many guns and grenades around."

Observers say Rakhmonov controls fully only 20 percent of the far-flung Central Asian state, whose tortuous borders touch China and Afghanistan along the treacherous passes of the Pamir mountains. Moscow, worried about radical Islam on its southern flank, keeps 20,000 frontier troops in Tajikistan.
Rakhmonov's peace talks with his armed Islamic opposition are at a standstill.
The guerrillas denied any link to Wednesday's attack but are fuming over what they say are government arrests of their people. A ceasefire agreed in December appears to be holding.
Diplomats and opposition sources say the attack could be revenge for the government's violent crushing of a prison riot in Khudjand earlier this month, which left 20 dead.
The riot leaders and Rakhmonov's would-be assassin were said by the authorities to have been involved in an anti-government demonstration in May last year.
The region is also base to a so-called "third force", excluded from a power-sharing arrangement tentatively agreed by the government and the Islamic opposition in February.
Observers say the Khudjand region and others in Tajikistan are frustrated with Rakhmonov's southern Kulyab clan, which holds a virtual monopoly on wealth and power.
Such seething regional and clan rivalries act as a catalyst to the republic's seemingly endless violence.
Rakhmonov also lives with a background threat of mutiny by the country's armed forces, unhappy at compromise with their erstwhile guerrilla enemies.
The commander of Rakhmonov's elite armoured brigade, Colonel Makhmud Khudoyberdyev, who is no fan of the peace negotiations, moves his tanks around at will.
Rakhmonov had to plead with him to return to barracks after one such jaunt in January and little was heard afterwards of a threat to court-martial the errant commander.
A confusion of armed bands and independent fiefdoms, fighting for a slice of the country's cotton, metals and narcotics wealth, pose a risk for Rakhmonov any time he ventures outside the capital.
He is not helped by what the diplomat said was a dangerous lack of security around the 45-year-old leader.
"The security is not even minimally adequate for a head of state in a country with such a high rate of violence," he said.
One wild-looking opposition band, rocket launchers on their backs and daggers in their belts, roams the foothills only 13 km (8 miles) from the capital.
Some aid agencies and diplomats have only just returned to the republic this month in the wake of a two-week hostage crisis in February in which several foreigners were kidnapped.
Tajikistan's war-weary population are the losers. Distribution of badly needed food and medicines is hampered by aid organisations' fears of further kidnappings and violence.
"We want to keep working here," said one aid worker in Dushanbe. "But if there's any more violence directed against us, it will be hard to convince headquarters to stay," she said.
